C270.notes: SER AS-JP-004. Value-side photo confirmed (portrait white 2×2 · EXIF-oriented) · user cue 昭和六十三年 / 1988 · big 10 inside a bay laurel wreath (Japan Mint: evergreen / tokiwa leaves; Wikipedia & Smithsonian: bay laurel — not tachibana, which rides the ¥500). Date kanji clearly 昭和六十三年 = Shōwa 63 = 1988. Byōdō-in Phoenix Hall / 日本国 / 十円 side not shown. Same Y#73a smooth-edge bronze type as C220 / AS-JP-003 (1982 Shōwa 57 10¥) — keep both; different year, not a duplicate. Aluminum 1¥ ladder siblings C222 / AS-JP-001 (1965) · C206 / AS-JP-002 (1976). Story hook: Shōwa 63 was the last full calendar year of the Shōwa era — Emperor Hirohito died 1989-01-07, so Shōwa 64 lasted only one week (1–7 Jan) before Heisei began 1989-01-08. Vending / train / konbini bronze weight in the final full year of a 62-year reign. Japan flips now 4.
C270.story: A 1988 10-yen coin from Japan. One side shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodoin temple with the country name (日本国) and value (十円). The other side shows a large 10, a wreath, and the Japanese Showa-era date (昭和 63, which is 1988). It is made of bronze (95% copper, 3–4% zinc, and 1–2% tin).

C340.notes: Both sides photographed. The value side reads 100 with the era date below it, read character by character from enlarged crops as Heisei 27 (2015). The blossom side carries the state name and the denomination in kanji around the flowers. Japan Mint; no mint letter on the type.
C340.story: A Japanese 100 yen coin dated Heisei 27 (2015). One side is filled with cherry blossoms, the sakura, Japan's beloved unofficial national flower; the other carries a big, plain 100. This design has served on the 100 yen since 1967, across three emperors.

C344.notes: Both sides photographed in the holder. Obverse: Phoenix Hall with the country name in kanji above and the value in kanji below. Reverse: big 10 inside a laurel wreath with the era date beneath in kanji, read as Heisei 14 (2002) glyph by glyph across enlarged and contrast-enhanced views; the year numeral is worn, so the year carries the caveat — era (Heisei) and the first three characters are clear, the fourth numeral reads as the boxed form of four. Bronze color and weight of the design rule out the aluminium 1 yen and brass 5 yen; the smooth edge and era name separate it from the collection's Showa strikes of the same type family.
C344.story: A Japanese 10 yen in bronze, dated Heisei 14 (2002), the fourteenth year of Emperor Akihito's reign. One side shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodoin temple in Uji, a thousand-year-old building so loved that it also appears on the 10,000 yen note. The other side frames a big 10 in a wreath of evergreen leaves. Japan has struck this design, nearly unchanged, since 1951, and it is still the 10 yen in everyday pockets today. The collection already holds two Showa-era strikes of the same design from 1982 and 1988; this is its first Heisei one.

issue.mint_text: Japan Mint; no mint mark (Japanese coinage carries none)

C353.notes: Both sides photographed in the holder. Transcription: obverse NIHON-KOKU (State of Japan) above the Phoenix Hall, JU-EN (ten yen) below; reverse the numeral 10 over HEISEI HACHI-NEN. The era year was read glyph-by-glyph from an enlarged crop: the numeral glyph is HACHI (eight), two splayed strokes, not ROKU (six) - Heisei 8 = 1996. The type line for this design was created in changes_muse_20261109-1725.jsonl (the 2002 specimen), still pending merge when this specimen was filed. Dark-toned bronze with light circulation wear.
C353.story: A Heisei-era ten yen piece, dated in the eighth year of Emperor Akihito's reign - 1996. The obverse shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodo-in temple at Uji, its wing-like roofs spread over the water it was built beside in 1053; the reverse carries the big 10 inside an evergreen-oak wreath, with the era date written out in kanji below. The same design has been on Japan's ten yen since 1959 and still circulates today; this one joins the Heisei 14 (2002) specimen filed from a chat photo the same day.
